statements.quote:
We developed a web application for participants to generate sup-
porting ideas with LLM at different stages of the ideation process.
We used Vue.js2 with Javascript3 for front-end development, and
took Django4 with Python5 to build the back-end server. This appli-
cation was installed on Heroku6 for public access during data col-
lection. Additionally, we adopted OpenAI’s GPT-47 API to build the
streaming content generation feature, aiming to maintain smooth
interaction and high-quality LLM responses.
statements.locator: p. 3, Section 3.4, Prototype for Generating Ideas with LLM (study software and public hosting during collection; not a data-release statement).

statements.quote:
Table 4 (see Appendix A) presents the outcome for a participant
from condition 𝐶𝑏𝑒𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑒interacting with the prototype for idea
generation. Throughout this process, AI provided nine ideas as
references, and the participant concluded by submitting three ideas.
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 3.4.1 continuation, referring to Appendix A, Table 4.

statements.quote:
To enable participants to easily generate supporting
ideas with LLM, we predefined three default prompts as examples
for participants to refer to. To standardize the responses and ensure
consistency across participants, each prompt was designed to elicit
four concise supporting ideas (each within 50 words).
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 3.4.2, Prompt Design for AI-assisted Ideation; three default prompts are printed immediately below.

statements.quote:
To answer our research questions, we collected quantitative data
from system logs and the questionnaire, as well as qualitative data
from participants’ open-ended responses.
statements.locator: p. 5, Section 3.5, Measurement (describes collected data; does not state availability).

statements.quote:
We also tried transformer-based embeddings (using the OpenAI text-embedding-ada-
002 model to embed each idea) for semantic similarity calculation while keeping the
other steps the same. It demonstrated a similar trend in the statistical analysis across
conditions, which did not alter the conclusion reached using TF-IDF. Please refer to
the Appendix A to see the result of using transformer-based methods to calculate
similarity scores (see Figure 7).
statements.locator: p. 5, footnote 8, referring to Appendix A, Figure 7.

statements.quote: Table 1: Pseudocode for calculating similarity scores between participant-generated and LLM-generated ideas.
statements.locator: p. 6, Table 1 caption (pseudocode printed in the paper; no code-repository link).

statements.quote:
This research work is partially supported by NUS IT’s Research
Computing group (NUSREC-HPC-00001) and AWS.

statements.locator: p. 15, Appendix A heading; the appendix continues through p. 16.

statements.quote:
Figure 7: Comparison between 𝐶𝑏𝑒𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑒and 𝐶𝑎𝑓𝑡𝑒𝑟in idea sim-
ilarity with LLM. (a) represents the detailed similarity distri-
bution, where the distribution of ideas generated by partici-
pants in 𝐶𝑎𝑓𝑡𝑒𝑟are concentrated in areas with lower scores
while that in 𝐶𝑏𝑒𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑒are comparatively higher. (b) depicts
that there is a significant difference caused by LLM usage
timing, which is consistent with the results in Figure 3. Sig-
nificant differences between the conditions are indicated by
p-value annotations, where ns >= 0.05, * < 0.05, ** < 0.01, *** <
0.001.
statements.locator: p. 15, Appendix A, Figure 7 caption (additional similarity plots).

statements.quote:
Table 4: An example of the ideation process using the experimental platform, which includes the prompt, participant-generated,
and LLM-generated ideas on the topic of the ‘jellyfish sting treatment’.
statements.locator: p. 16, Appendix A, Table 4 caption (one participant example, not the study dataset).

notes:
Read all 86,123 characters / 582 lines of the markdown conversion, including references and Appendix A, against the 16-page saved preprint. Verified relevant passages directly with PyMuPDF text extraction from PDF pages 3, 5, 6, 13, 15 and 16. Quotes retain PDF text-layer line breaks, hyphenation and footnote numerals; they are not availability promises.

No statement offers public or on-request participant data, executable analysis code, a project-specific study-materials repository, or preregistration. The screening form's data_url and code_url are both empty. Recorded statements cover the related software, collected-data and in-paper supplementary-materials passages so these are not mistaken for a release.

Appendix A is inside the paper: Figure 7 provides additional similarity plots, and Table 4 prints one C_before participant's prompt, three submitted ideas and nine LLM-generated ideas. It does not identify that participant, provide a study-wide data table, contain the remaining participants' texts, or give participant outcome scores. Section 3.4.2 prints three default prompts and Table 1 prints pseudocode. These in-paper examples, prompts and pseudocode are not counted as an independent data/code/materials deposit. The Heroku statement concerns access to the study application during collection and supplies only Heroku's homepage, not a project or dataset URL.

No relevant data deposit was identified by the recorded title/first-author searches in DataCite, Zenodo, Harvard Dataverse or OSF. Therefore there was no relevant repository identifier for a files/children API listing and no data file to inspect in memory. No GitHub repository is named in the paper, so no GitHub API requests were used. The article-only arXiv result is documented in searches but excluded from deposits.

Publisher verification remains incomplete: the publication DOI and direct ACM landing-page requests returned HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' bot check. Stopped there; no login, access request or bypass was attempted. This does not establish that any dataset is restricted or absent. As an independent named source, the arXiv landing page returned HTTP 200, identifies only v1 submitted 10 February 2025, and links the same ACM DOI; it names no project-specific dataset, code repository or external supplement. Generic arXiv Code/Data/Media service widgets were not interpreted as deposits.

All unique HTTP URLs printed in the paper were checked, including generic software/service documentation and the placeholder DOI. HTTP checks: https://doi.org/10.1145/nnnnnnn.nnnnnnn -> HTTP 404; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript -> HTTP 200; https://jasp-stats.org/ -> HTTP 200; https://openai.com/index/gpt-4/ -> HTTP 403; https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/embeddings -> HTTP 403; https://vuejs.org/ -> HTTP 200; https://www.djangoproject.com/ -> HTTP 200; https://www.heroku.com/ -> HTTP 200; https://www.prolific.co/ -> HTTP 200 (final URL https://www.prolific.com/); https://www.python.org/ -> HTTP 200; https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713146 -> HTTP 403 (final URL https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713146); https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713146 -> HTTP 403; https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06197 -> HTTP 200. The placeholder DOI 10.1145/nnnnnnn.nnnnnnn is a dead publication placeholder, not a data link. The two OpenAI documentation/product URLs also returned 403 and were not bypassed.

No newly located public data permit computing S1 arm means, SDs or SEs for within-person diversity, confirming per-arm analyzed counts from records, recounting LLM suggestions by arm (final.open_items item 3), separating ideas written before AI access (item 6), checking the inconsistent similarity t (item 1), or establishing the diversity sign convention (item 8). No study-wide texts were located for across-participant diversity/homogenization analysis. what_we_could_compute is null because no usable public dataset was confirmed; statistics derivable from already printed aggregates are outside this data-availability finding.

Confidence is medium: the saved full text and successful repository searches support none_found, but the ACM bot check prevents ruling out publisher-only supplementary data, and searches cannot rule out an unindexed deposit.
